title: The dispute over whether all acts of the will are free is a mere quarrel about words
source_text: XXV. Unde patet, ut agnoscit Strangius loco citato, λογομαχίαν meram esse inter eos qui affirmant omnes voluntatis actiones liberas esse, & inter eos qui liberas esse negant. Nam qui istud affirmant libertatem late sumunt pro libentia illa qua voluntas ultro sequitur judicium intellectus, quo sensu nemo est qui neget omnem omnino voluntatis actionem liberam esse. Qui autem istud negant, libertatem accipiunt pro illa per naturam indeterminatione, & indifferentia, quae voluntati competit respectu actuum illorum qui sub deliberationem & consultationem cadunt. Quo sensu manifestum est, & ab omnibus concessum voluntatem liberam non esse respectu quorundam ipsius actuum. Sed cum latior ista libertatis acceptio minus recepta sit atque usitata, quantum autem fieri potest cum pluribus loquendum sit, quando simpliciter loquimur, omnino convenit, ut potius negemus, quam affirmemus voluntatem liberam esse in iis actibus, circa quos priorem tantum, non vero posteriorem & stricte dictam libertatem exercet.
pass_a_gloss: Whence it is plain, as Strang acknowledges in the place cited, that there is a mere logomachy between those who affirm all actions of the will to be free, & between those who deny them to be free. For those who affirm this take liberty broadly for that willingness by which the will of its own accord follows the judgement of the intellect, in which sense there is no one who would deny every action of the will whatever to be free. But those who deny this, take liberty for that indetermination by nature, & indifference, which belongs to the will in respect of those acts which fall under deliberation & consultation. In which sense it is manifest, & granted by all that the will is not free in respect of certain of its acts. But since that broader acceptation of liberty is less received and usual, and as far as can be done one must speak with the many, when we speak simply, it is altogether fitting, that we rather deny, than affirm the will to be free in those acts, about which it exercises only the former, but not the latter & strictly so called liberty.
pass_b_english: So it is clear, as Strang admits in the passage cited, that the dispute between those who say all the will's acts are free and those who deny it is merely a quarrel about words (logomachia).

Those who say so take freedom broadly, as the willingness with which the will readily follows the intellect's judgement; in that sense no one would deny that every act of the will without exception is free. Those who deny it take freedom as the openness and indifference by nature that the will has toward acts that come under weighing and deliberation. In that sense it is obvious, and everyone grants, that the will is not free with respect to some of its acts.

But the broader use of 'freedom' is less accepted and less common, and we should speak with the majority as far as we can. So when we speak without qualification, it is entirely proper to deny rather than affirm that the will is free in acts where it exercises only the first kind of freedom and not the second, strict kind.

choices.english: we should speak with the majority
choices.why: The maxim is to follow common usage in speech; 'speak with the majority' keeps it close.
